chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
title: Being pushed to play blues after the hit
summary: The record's success forced them to play vocal blues behind Brown, though before it their blues were instrumental, and live versions ran five to six minutes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It pushed you a little bit in a direction you were not going.

It actually did. That is true. It pushed us because you would be surprised, the places we would play, we'd come in with a big band and they would say, man, we never thought you all had a band anything like this. We expected to see about four musicians and hear Brown singing the blues. They say, what, people were just turned around.
And -- but like you said, we are forced to play the blues, you know what I mean. We are forced to play the blues. Well, at that time, to tell you the truth, we hadn't been playing no blues.
What about all these heads you had, weren't they blues.
I mean up until we made our first recording we hadn't been playing blues. No, in Kansas City --
A lot of things, the head arrangements you had, weren't they blues.

Yes, but those were instrumental blues, like Jump Blues. Built on that form, not the other form blues, you know, and so yes, we had been playing the blues, but in a different category of blues. Like One O'clock Jump, that's the blues but people don't -- you ask the average person, they say, oh, that's One O'clock Jump. But it's the blues. But that's the type of thing that we had been doing.

But consequently this made us have to play the other blues too, so then we put other arrangements behind Brown and started getting tunes and other blues and things together, Four Day Rider and things like that, One Woman's Man Blues.
Did Charlie play -- take choruses back of those -- bird Yarborough.
Did he take choruses in there, that kind of blues.
Oh, yes. You see, just like on 'Acorn' Blues, Charlie blew a solo in there.
I Suppose to, when you played in person, it wasn't always -- it wasn't exactly the same as the record, was it.

That's right. And see, now when we're playing in person, whereas the record is a three-minute record, back in them days, a three-minute record. When we played Hootie Blues, Confessin' or any of those Brown blues, they lasted five to six minutes, because they way we did it.
